title: Ἀλώπηξ ⟨μηδέποτε θεασαμένη λέοντα⟩
titleEn: The Fox Who Had Never Seen a Lion
part: The Fox Who Had Never Seen a Lion (Chambry 42 · Perry 10)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 42 (= Perry 10). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ μηδέποτε θεασαμένη λέοντα, ἐπειδὴ κατά τινα συντυχίαν ὑπήντησε, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἰδοῦσα οὕτως διεταράχθη ὡς μικροῦ καὶ ἀποθανεῖν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx mēdepote theasamenē leonta, epeidē kata tina syntychian hypēntēse, to men prōton idousa houtōs dietarachthē hōs mikrou kai apothanein.
sentences.l: A fox who had never beheld a lion, when by some chance she met him, the first time, on seeing him, was so thrown into confusion as almost to die.
sentences.i: A fox who had never seen a lion happened by some chance to meet one; and the first time she saw him she was so shaken that she all but died.
sentences.n: μή rather than οὐ with the participle (μηδέποτε θεασαμένη) makes the description general — the sort of fox that has never seen one — rather than a denial of fact. οὕτως … ὡς with the infinitive is the result construction, “so … as to”; μικροῦ, “by a little,” is a genitive of measure and means “almost.” τὸ μὲν πρῶτον is adverbial, and its μέν is answered not by a δέ in this sentence but by the two that follow: first time, second time, third.

sentences.t: Ἐκ δευτέρου δὲ αὐτῷ περιτυχοῦσα ἐφοβήθη μέν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ οὕτως ὡς τὸ πρότερον.
sentences.tr: Ek deuterou de autōi peritychousa ephobēthē men, all’ ouch houtōs hōs to proteron.
sentences.l: And meeting with him a second time she was afraid, indeed, but not so much as the former time.
sentences.n: μέν answered by ἀλλά rather than the usual δέ: the concession granted (“afraid, yes”) and then corrected. ἐκ δευτέρου, ἐκ τρίτου — “on the second, on the third occasion.”

sentences.t: Ἐκ τρίτου δὲ θεασαμένη οὕτω κατεθάρρησεν ὡς καὶ προσελθοῦσα αὐτῷ διελέχθη.
sentences.tr: Ek tritou de theasamenē houtō katetharrēsen hōs kai proselthousa autōi dielechthē.
sentences.l: And beholding him a third time she took such courage that she even went up to him and conversed with him.
sentences.n: The result clause here takes the indicative (ὡς … διελέχθη), where the first sentence took the infinitive: Greek distinguishes the result that actually happened from the result a thing merely tends to — a distinction English cannot make without adding words. κατεθάρρησεν is an aorist of entering the state, “grew bold.”

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἡ συνήθεια καὶ τὰ φοβερὰ τῶν πραγμάτων καταπραύνει.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hē synētheia kai ta phobera tōn pragmatōn katapraynei.
sentences.l: The story shows that familiarity makes gentle even the fearful among things.
sentences.i: The story shows that familiarity takes the terror even out of frightening things.
sentences.n: συνήθεια is being used to a thing, the habit that repetition builds. καί here is “even,” not “and.” τὰ φοβερὰ τῶν πραγμάτων, “the frightening ones of things,” is a partitive genitive under a neuter adjective — the same shape as τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ πονηροί, which these morals use constantly. The verb is καταπραΰνω, where the υ is a syllable of its own (πραΰς, “gentle”); the diaeresis is not printed here, and the romanization follows the word rather than the printed form.
